smt-2020-power-01.title: Take $A=B=1$
smt-2020-power-01.body: With $Q(x)=x+1$ we get $q_i=i$, which lists all non-negative integers; so every residue class modulo $10^k$ occurs, for every $k$. ∎

smt-2020-power-02a.title: Induction
smt-2020-power-02a.body: If $A=1$ then $q_{n+1}=q_n+B$, so $q_n=nB$. If $A\ne1$, the claim $q_n=B\frac{A^n-1}{A-1}$ holds for $n=0$ and, if it holds for $n$, $q_{n+1}=A\cdot B\frac{A^n-1}{A-1}+B=B\frac{A^{n+1}-A+A-1}{A-1}=B\frac{A^{n+1}-1}{A-1}$. ∎

smt-2020-power-03a.title: Look at the maps mod 5 and mod 2
smt-2020-power-03a.body:
Suppose all residues mod $10$ occur; then all residues mod $5$ occur.

*Mod 5.* Let $f(x)=Ax+B$ on $\mathbb Z_5$. If $A\equiv0$ then $q_i\equiv B$ for $i\ge1$, so at most the residues $0,B$ occur, not all $5$. If $A\not\equiv0,1\pmod 5$, $f$ is a bijection of $\mathbb Z_5$ with a fixed point $x_0=B/(1-A)$; if $x_0\ne0$, the orbit of $0$ never reaches $x_0$ (a bijection cannot send another point to a fixed point), and if $x_0=0$ the sequence is constantly $0$. Either way not all residues occur. So $A\equiv1\pmod5$, i.e. $A\equiv1$ or $6\pmod{10}$.

*Excluding $A\equiv6\pmod{10}$.* Then $A$ is even, so $q_i\equiv B\pmod2$ for all $i\ge1$. Together with $q_0=0$, only the residues of one parity (plus $0$) occur modulo $10$, so some residue class is missed.

Hence $A\equiv1\pmod{10}$. ∎

smt-2020-power-03b.title: Reduce mod 4
smt-2020-power-03b.body: $q_n=B\frac{11^n-1}{10}=B\sum_{k\ge1}\binom nk10^{k-1}=B\left(n+10\binom n2+100(\cdots)\right)\equiv B\bigl(n+5n(n-1)\bigr)\pmod{100}$. Reducing modulo $4$ ($5\equiv1$): $q_n\equiv B(n+n(n-1))=Bn^2\pmod4$. Since $n^2\equiv0$ or $1\pmod4$, $q_n$ takes at most two of the four residues modulo $4$. So at most half of the residue classes modulo $100$ (those with the residues mod $4$ seen) can occur. ∎

smt-2020-power-04a.title: Use $q_n\equiv n+10n(n-1)\pmod{100}$
smt-2020-power-04a.body:
(Derived in part (c).) With $q_n\equiv n+10n(n-1)\pmod{100}$ we get, for column $a=9$ ($n=81,\dots,90$): $q_{81}\equiv81$, $q_{82}\equiv02$, $q_{83}\equiv43$, $q_{84}\equiv04$, $q_{85}\equiv85$, $q_{86}\equiv86$, $q_{87}\equiv07$, $q_{88}\equiv48$, $q_{89}\equiv09$, $q_{90}\equiv90$.

For column $a=10$ ($n=91,\dots,100$): $q_{91}\equiv91$, $q_{92}\equiv12$, $q_{93}\equiv53$, $q_{94}\equiv14$, $q_{95}\equiv95$, $q_{96}\equiv96$, $q_{97}\equiv17$, $q_{98}\equiv58$, $q_{99}\equiv19$, $q_{100}\equiv00$.

(One can check the printed columns the same way, e.g. $q_{71}\equiv71$, $q_{10}\equiv10$.)

smt-2020-power-04b.title: Reduce mod 10
smt-2020-power-04b.body: $Q(x)=21x+1\equiv x+1\pmod{10}$, so $q_i\equiv i\pmod{10}$. All residues occur. ∎

smt-2020-power-04c.title: Binomial expansion
smt-2020-power-04c.body: $q_n=\frac{21^n-1}{20}=\frac{(1+20)^n-1}{20}=\sum_{k\ge1}\binom nk20^{k-1}=n+20\binom n2+400\binom n3+\cdots\equiv n+10n(n-1)\pmod{100}$. So $f(n)=n(n-1)$ works. ∎

smt-2020-power-04d.title: Shift by 10
smt-2020-power-04d.body: By (c), $q_{n+10}-q_n\equiv10+10\left[(n+10)(n+9)-n(n-1)\right]=10+10(20n+90)\equiv10\pmod{100}$. Given a target residue $r$, choose $n_0\in\{0,\dots,9\}$ with $n_0\equiv r\pmod{10}$ (possible since $q_{n_0}\equiv n_0\pmod{10}$). Then $q_{n_0+10m}\equiv q_{n_0}+10m\pmod{100}$, and $r-q_{n_0}$ is a multiple of $10$, so some $m$ gives $q_{n_0+10m}\equiv r\pmod{100}$. ∎

smt-2020-power-04e.title: Induction on $k$
smt-2020-power-04e.body:
Write $A=21$, so $q_n=\frac{A^n-1}{20}$ and $q_{n+N}-q_n=A^nq_N$. Put $N_k=10^k$.

*Claim:* $q_{N_k}=10^kw_k$ with $w_k\equiv1\pmod{10}$ for all $k\ge1$. For $k=1$: $q_{10}\equiv10\pmod{100}$ by (c), so $w_1\equiv1$. For the step ($k\ge1$): $\frac{q_{10N}}{q_N}=\frac{A^{10N}-1}{A^N-1}=\sum_{i=0}^9A^{iN}$ with $N=N_k$. Since $A^N-1=20q_N$ is a multiple of $200$, $A^{iN}\equiv1+i(A^N-1)\pmod{(A^N-1)^2}$, so the sum is $\equiv10+45(A^N-1)\equiv10\pmod{100}$. Hence $q_{N_{k+1}}=q_{N_k}\cdot(10+100m)=10q_{N_k}(1+10m)$, i.e. $w_{k+1}=w_k(1+10m)\equiv w_k\equiv1\pmod{10}$.

*Covering:* Suppose all residues mod $10^k$ occur ($k=1$ is (b)). Since $A\equiv1\pmod{10}$, each step of $10^k$ in the index adds $A^{m}q_{N_k}\equiv10^kw_k\equiv10^k\pmod{10^{k+1}}$, so $q_{n+jN_k}\equiv q_n+j\cdot10^k\pmod{10^{k+1}}$; also $q_{n+jN_k}\equiv q_n\pmod{10^k}$. Given a target $r$ modulo $10^{k+1}$, pick $n$ with $q_n\equiv r\pmod{10^k}$; then $r-q_n\equiv10^kt\pmod{10^{k+1}}$ for some $t$, and $j\equiv t\pmod{10}$ gives $q_{n+jN_k}\equiv r\pmod{10^{k+1}}$. By induction all residues modulo every $10^k$ occur. ∎

smt-2020-power-05a.title: Pigeonhole
smt-2020-power-05a.body: There are only $p^{k+1}$ residues, so $q_i\equiv q_j\pmod{p^{k+1}}$ for some $i<j$. Since $Q$ has integer coefficients, congruent inputs give congruent outputs, so $q_{i+s}\equiv q_{j+s}$ for all $s\ge0$. Take $N=i$, $t=j-i$. ∎

smt-2020-power-05b.title: The residue 0 recurs
smt-2020-power-05b.body: All $p^k$ residues mod $p^k$ occur, in particular the $p^{k-j}\ge p\ge2$ residues that are $\equiv0\pmod{p^j}$, each at some index (different indices, since the values differ). So there are two indices $0\le i<i'$ with $q_i\equiv q_{i'}\equiv0\pmod{p^j}$; replacing $i$ by the smallest one: index $0$ itself is one ($q_0=0$), so there is $t\ge1$ with $q_t\equiv0\equiv q_0\pmod{p^j}$. Then $q_{t+n}=Q^{n}(q_t)\equiv Q^n(q_0)=q_n\pmod{p^j}$ for all $n$. ∎

smt-2020-power-05c.title: The map is a single cycle
smt-2020-power-05c.body:
Let $f$ denote $x\mapsto Q(x)$ acting on $\mathbb Z/p^k$. The orbit of $0$ contains all $p^k$ residues, so $q_0,\dots,q_{p^k-1}$ are distinct mod $p^k$ and every residue other than possibly $q_0=0$ is in the image of $f$. We show $f$ is a permutation.

*$f$ is a permutation mod $p$.* Otherwise the image of $f$ mod $p$ has at most $p-1$ residues. Then the image of $f$ mod $p^k$ lies in at most $p-1$ of the $p$ fibres, missing at least $p^{k-1}\ge2$ residues. But only $0$ can fail to be in the image. Contradiction.

*$f'(x)\not\equiv0\pmod p$ for all $x$.* For $k\ge2$, $f(x+p^{k-1}y)\equiv f(x)+p^{k-1}yf'(x)\pmod{p^k}$ (expand $Q$; the quadratic term has $p^{2k-2}$, divisible by $p^k$). If $f'(x_0)\equiv0\pmod p$ then, as $f'\bmod p$ depends only on $x\bmod p$, for every $x\equiv x_0\pmod p$ the $p$ residues $x+p^{k-1}y$ have the same image. That loses at least $(p-1)p^{k-2}\ge2$ residues from the image (as $k\ge8$), again impossible.

*$f$ is injective mod $p^k$.* If $f(x)\equiv f(x')\pmod{p^k}$ then $x\equiv x'\pmod p$ (permutation mod $p$), and $f(x)-f(x')=(x-x')D$ with $D\equiv f'(x)\not\equiv0\pmod p$, so $p^k\mid x-x'$.

So $f$ is a permutation of $\mathbb Z/p^k$ whose orbit of $0$ is everything: a single cycle of length $p^k$. Reducing modulo $p^j$ ($j\le k$), $f$ is a permutation of $\mathbb Z/p^j$ which is still one cycle (the orbit of $0$ covers everything), of length exactly $p^j$. Hence $q_n\equiv q_m\pmod{p^j}$ iff $n\equiv m\pmod{p^j}$: the minimal period is $p^j$ (a period $t$ must satisfy $q_t\equiv q_0$, so $p^j\mid t$). ∎

smt-2020-power-07.title: Use the exact period
smt-2020-power-07.body: By 5(c) ($j\le k$), $q_n\equiv q_0=0\pmod{p^j}$ iff $p^j\mid n$ (the minimal period is $p^j$ and $q_i\equiv0$ exactly at multiples of the period). Let $v=v_p(n)\le k-1$. Then $p^v\mid n$ gives $p^v\mid q_n$, and $p^{v+1}\nmid n$ with $v+1\le k$ gives $p^{v+1}\nmid q_n$. So $v_p(q_n)=v$. ∎

smt-2020-power-08a.title: Binomial expansion
smt-2020-power-08a.body: For $P=\sum a_ix^i$: $(x+zp^n)^i=x^i+ix^{i-1}zp^n+\binom i2x^{i-2}z^2p^{2n}+\cdots\equiv x^i+i\,x^{i-1}zp^n\pmod{p^{2n}}$. Summing, $P(x+zp^n)\equiv P(x)+zp^n\sum ia_ix^{i-1}$, so $R=P'\in\mathbb Z[x]$ works. ∎

smt-2020-power-08b.title: Compose $Q$ with itself $p^{k-2}$ times
smt-2020-power-08b.body:
Let $m=p^{k-2}$ and $P=Q^{\circ m}$ ($m$-fold composition, a polynomial in $\mathbb Z[x]$), so $q_{nm}=P(q_{(n-1)m})$ and $q_m=P(0)$. By 5(c), $p^{k-2}\mid q_{(n-1)m}$ because $p^{k-2}\mid(n-1)m$; write $q_{(n-1)m}=zp^{k-2}$. By 8(a) with exponent $k-2$ and $x=0$:
$$q_{nm}=P(0+zp^{k-2})\equiv P(0)+zp^{k-2}R(0)=q_m+R(0)\,q_{(n-1)m}\pmod{p^{2(k-2)}},$$
and $2(k-2)\ge k+2$ since $k\ge6$. So $\alpha=R(0)$ works; if $R(0)=1$ use $\alpha=1+p^{k+2}$ instead, which changes nothing modulo $p^{k+2}$. ∎

smt-2020-power-08c.title: Induction
smt-2020-power-08c.body: Write $m=p^{k-2}$. For $n=1$ both sides equal $q_m$. If $q_{nm}\equiv(1+\alpha+\dots+\alpha^{n-1})q_m$, then $q_{(n+1)m}\equiv q_m+\alpha q_{nm}\equiv\bigl(1+\alpha+\dots+\alpha^n\bigr)q_m\pmod{p^{k+2}}$. ∎

smt-2020-power-09b.title: Extend using the $\alpha$-formula
smt-2020-power-09b.body:
Let $m=p^{k-2}$ and $v=v_p(n)$. If $v\le k-1$ the claim is 7. Assume $k-2\le v\le k+1$ and write $n=mt$, $v_p(t)=v-(k-2)\in\{0,1,2,3\}$. By 8(c), $q_n\equiv S_t\,q_m\pmod{p^{k+2}}$ with $S_t=1+\alpha+\dots+\alpha^{t-1}$, and $v_p(q_m)=k-2$ by 7.

*Claim: $v_p(S_t)=v_p(t)$ for all $t\ge1$.* Taking $n=pm$ (valuation $k-1$, covered by 7) gives $v_p(q_{pm})=k-1$, and $q_{pm}\equiv S_pq_m\pmod{p^{k+2}}$, so $v_p(S_p)=1$. In particular $p\mid S_p=\frac{\alpha^p-1}{\alpha-1}$. If $\alpha\not\equiv1\pmod p$, then since $\alpha^p\equiv\alpha$, $S_p\equiv1\pmod p$, impossible. So $p\mid\alpha-1$ (and for $p=2$: $S_2=1+\alpha$ has $v_2=1$, so $\alpha\equiv1\pmod4$). Now LTE gives $v_p(\alpha^t-1)=v_p(t)+v_p(\alpha-1)$, hence $v_p(S_t)=v_p(t)$.

Therefore $v_p(S_tq_m)=v_p(t)+k-2=v\le k+1<k+2$, and since $q_n\equiv S_tq_m\pmod{p^{k+2}}$ has valuation below $k+2$, $v_p(q_n)=v$. ∎

smt-2020-power-09c.title: First return to 0
smt-2020-power-09c.body: For $0<n<p^{k+1}$ we have $v_p(n)\le k$, so $v_p(q_n)=v_p(n)\le k$ and $q_n\not\equiv0\pmod{p^{k+1}}$; for $n=p^{k+1}$, $v_p(q_n)=k+1$, so $q_n\equiv0\pmod{p^{k+1}}$. Hence $q_{p^{k+1}}\equiv q_0$, and so $q_{n+p^{k+1}}\equiv q_n$ for all $n$ (apply $Q$ repeatedly), and no smaller $t>0$ has $q_t\equiv q_0$. So the sequence is purely periodic with minimal period $p^{k+1}$; its first $p^{k+1}$ terms are pairwise distinct (a purely periodic orbit of a map has distinct values over a minimal period), so all $p^{k+1}$ residues occur. ∎

smt-2020-power-10.title: Prime by prime
smt-2020-power-10.body:
Let $n=p_1^{\beta_1}\cdots p_s^{\beta_s}$. All residues mod $n^k$ occur, hence all residues mod $p_i^{k\beta_i}$ occur, with $k\beta_i\ge8$. By 5(c) (for exponents up to $k\beta_i$) and by repeated use of 9(c) (for larger exponents), for every $j\ge1$ the sequence mod $p_i^{j}$ is purely periodic with minimal period $p_i^{j}$ and contains all residues mod $p_i^j$.

Fix $l$ and a target residue $r$. For each $i$ there is $m_i$ with $q_{m}\equiv r\pmod{p_i^{l\beta_i}}$ for every $m\equiv m_i\pmod{p_i^{l\beta_i}}$ (periodicity). The moduli $p_i^{l\beta_i}$ are coprime, so by the Chinese Remainder Theorem there is $m$ with $m\equiv m_i\pmod{p_i^{l\beta_i}}$ for all $i$. Then $q_m\equiv r\pmod{p_i^{l\beta_i}}$ for all $i$, hence $q_m\equiv r\pmod{n^l}$. ∎

smt-2020-power-11a.title: Powers of two
smt-2020-power-11a.body: Let $S=\{2^j:j\ge0\}$ and suppose $2^a<2^b<2^c$ form an arithmetic progression. Then $2^{b+1}=2^a+2^c=2^a(1+2^{c-a})$. The factor $1+2^{c-a}$ is odd and greater than $1$, but $2^{b+1-a}$ has no odd divisor $>1$. Contradiction. ∎

smt-2020-power-11b.title: Random colouring
smt-2020-power-11b.body:
Let $N=10^{100}=100^{50}$ and colour each element of $\{1,\dots,N\}$ independently and uniformly with one of $100$ colours. A given $101$-term arithmetic progression is monochromatic with probability $100\cdot100^{-101}=100^{-100}$. The number of $101$-term progressions $a,a+d,\dots,a+100d\subseteq[1,N]$ is the number of pairs $(a,d)$ with $a,d\ge1$ and $a+100d\le N$, which is less than $N\cdot\frac N{100}<N^2=100^{100}$. So the expected number of monochromatic progressions is less than $100^{100}\cdot100^{-100}=1$. Hence some colouring has none; the $100$ colour classes are the required partition. ∎

(The official solution counts the same way: there are $100^N$ colourings and fewer than $N^2\cdot100^{N-100}$ of them contain a monochromatic progression.)

smt-2020-power-12a.title: Blocks as letters
smt-2020-power-12a.body: Let $W$ be a binary word and $m\in\mathbb N$. Define $W'$ with letters $w'_i=w_iw_{i+1}\cdots w_{i+m-1}$ (a letter from an alphabet of $2^m$ symbols). By (A) with $r=2^m$, some symbol $u$ appears in $W'$ at indices $a,a+d,\dots,a+(k-1)d$; that means the length-$m$ word $u$ appears in $W$ at these indices. ∎

smt-2020-power-12b.title: Binary encoding
smt-2020-power-12b.body:
Let $W$ be an infinite word on letters $1,\dots,r$. Encode letter $i$ by the block $c_i=1^i0^{r+1-i}$ of length $L=r+1$ (it starts with $1$ and ends with $0$) and let $\widetilde W$ be the binary word obtained by concatenating the blocks of the letters of $W$. In $\widetilde W$ each block begins right after a "$0$" (or at the start) and starts with $1$, so block starts inside $\widetilde W$ are exactly the places where "$01$" occurs, plus index $0$.

Apply (B) with $m=2L$: some word $u$ of length $2L$ appears in $\widetilde W$ at indices $a,a+d,\dots,a+(k-1)d$. In $u$ look at its first occurrence of "$01$" at offset $s$ (it exists and the block start $s+1$ is at most $L$, since every block ends in $0$ and the next begins with $1$). In every copy, position $a+jd+s+1$ is therefore a block start, and the whole block starting there ($L$ letters, offsets $s+1,\dots,s+L\le2L-1$) lies inside the copy of $u$, so it is the same block $c_i$ in every copy. Block starts are multiples of $L$, so $L\mid d$ and the letter $i$ appears in $W$ at the $k$ indices $\frac{a+s+1}L+j\frac dL$ ($j<k$), an arithmetic progression with positive difference. ∎

smt-2020-power-13a.title: Truncate
smt-2020-power-13a.body: Let $F$ be the set of letters occurring only finitely often in $W$ and let $M$ exceed the index of the last occurrence of any letter of $F$ (there are finitely many letters). Put $W^*=T^M(W)$. Every finite subword of $W^*$ is a subword of $W$, so $W^*\prec W$. Every letter in $W^*$ is not in $F$, so it occurs infinitely often in $W$, hence infinitely often (beyond index $M$) in $W^*$. ∎

smt-2020-power-13b.title: Truncate past rare words
smt-2020-power-13b.body: There are finitely many words of length at most $m$. Let $F$ be those that occur only finitely often in $W$, and let $M$ be larger than the largest index at which a word of $F$ occurs. Let $W^*=T^M(W)$. Then $W^*\prec W$, and a word $u$ of length at most $m$ appearing in $W^*$ is not in $F$ (no word of $F$ occurs at an index $\ge M$), so $u$ occurs infinitely often in $W$, hence at infinitely many indices $\ge M$, i.e. infinitely often in $W^*$. ∎

smt-2020-power-13c.title: Sparse ones
smt-2020-power-13c.body: Let $W$ have the letter $1$ at the indices $2^j$ ($j\ge0$) and $0$ elsewhere. The gaps between consecutive ones are $2^{j}-2^{j-1}-1=2^{j-1}-1$ zeros, all different. For $\ell\ge1$ choose $j$ with $2^{j-1}>\ell$ and let $w_\ell=1\,0^{2^{j-1}-1}1$. It appears in $W$ exactly once (at the index $2^{j-1}$), which is beyond $\ell$, so it appears exactly once, in particular finitely often, in $T^\ell(W)$. ∎

smt-2020-power-14.title: Blocks
smt-2020-power-14.body: The block between the $n$-th and $(n+1)$-st $c$ is the alternating word of length $n$ starting with $a$, which is exactly the length-$n$ prefix of $W'$. A finite subword of $W'$ lies in some prefix of $W'$, so it lies in one of these blocks, hence appears in $W$. ∎

smt-2020-power-15a.title: Universal word
smt-2020-power-15a.body: Let $X=U_1U_2U_3\cdots$ where $U_m$ is the concatenation of all words of length $m$ over the alphabet. Given $W$, for each $m$ the prefix of $W$ of length $m$ occurs inside $U_m$ at some index $n_m$ of $X$; since the blocks $U_m$ come one after the other, $n_1\le n_2\le\cdots$ (indeed $n_m$ lies in $U_m$, which lies after $U_{m-1}$). Then $T^{n_m}(X)$ agrees with $W$ in its first $m$ letters, so $T^{n_m}(X)\to W$. ∎

smt-2020-power-15b.title: Both directions
smt-2020-power-15b.body:
(⇒) Suppose $T^{n_i}(W)\to W^*$ and let $u$ be a finite subword of $W^*$, lying in its first $M$ letters. For large $i$ the first $M$ letters of $T^{n_i}(W)$ equal those of $W^*$, so $u$ appears in $T^{n_i}(W)$ and hence in $W$.

(⇐) Suppose $W^*\prec W$. For each $m$ the length-$m$ prefix of $W^*$ appears in $W$, at some index $k_m$; so $T^{k_m}(W)$ agrees with $W^*$ on its first $m$ letters. Every sequence of natural numbers has a non-decreasing subsequence (if unbounded, take an increasing one; if bounded, some value repeats infinitely often). Take $m_1<m_2<\cdots$ with $k_{m_1}\le k_{m_2}\le\cdots$. Then $T^{k_{m_i}}(W)$ agrees with $W^*$ on the first $m_i$ letters, so it converges to $W^*$. So $W^*$ is a T-limit of $W$. ∎

smt-2020-power-15c.title: Reduce to inclusion
smt-2020-power-15c.body: Let $u$ be a finite subword of $X^*$, inside its first $M$ letters. Since $X_n\to X^*$, for large $n$ the first $M$ letters of $X_n$ agree with those of $X^*$, so $u$ is a subword of $X_n$. As $X_n$ is a T-limit of $W$, $X_n\prec W$ (15(b), direction ⇒), so $u$ appears in $W$. Thus $X^*\prec W$, and by 15(b) (⇐) $X^*$ is a T-limit of $W$. ∎

smt-2020-power-16a.title: Pigeonhole
smt-2020-power-16a.body: There are finitely many letters and infinitely many words, so some letter $a_0$ is the first letter of infinitely many $W_i$. Those words form the subsequence. ∎

smt-2020-power-16b.title: Pigeonhole again
smt-2020-power-16b.body: Among the infinitely many words $W^{(1)}_i$, some letter $a_1$ occurs as the second letter in infinitely many of them; take those. ∎

smt-2020-power-16c.title: Diagonal subsequence
smt-2020-power-16c.body: By repeating the pigeonhole of 16(a),(b) we get nested subsequences $S^{(1)}\supseteq S^{(2)}\supseteq\cdots$ of the original sequence such that all words of $S^{(j)}$ start with the same $j$ letters $a_0a_1\cdots a_{j-1}$. Let $A=a_0a_1a_2\cdots$. Choose from $S^{(1)}$ a word $V_1$, from $S^{(2)}$ a word $V_2$ with a larger original index than $V_1$, and so on ($V_j\in S^{(j)}$ with indices strictly increasing, possible since each $S^{(j)}$ is infinite). The first $j$ letters of $V_j,V_{j+1},\dots$ are $a_0\cdots a_{j-1}$, so $V_j\to A$. Thus $A$ is a strict limit. ∎

smt-2020-power-17.title: Strict limit of truncations
smt-2020-power-17.body: By 16(c) the sequence $T^0(W),T^1(W),T^2(W),\dots$ has a strict limit $W^*$: there are $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ with $T^{n_i}(W)\to W^*$. By 15(b), $W^*\prec W$. If a finite word $u$ appears in $W^*$ (within its first $M$ letters), then for all large $i$ the first $M$ letters of $T^{n_i}(W)$ contain $u$, so $u$ appears in $W$ at an index $\ge n_i$. Since $n_i\to\infty$, $u$ appears in $W$ at infinitely many indices. ∎

smt-2020-power-18a.title: Pigeonhole
smt-2020-power-18a.body: Among the first $r+1$ letters two are equal, at indices $i<j$; these form a $2$-term arithmetic progression of the same letter. So $N(r,2)=r+1$ works. ∎

smt-2020-power-18b.title: Contradiction via strict limit
smt-2020-power-18b.body: Suppose for some $r,k$ no $N$ works. Then for every $N$ there is an infinite word $W_N$ on $r$ letters whose first $N$ letters contain no monochromatic $k$-term progression. By 16(c) there is a strict limit $W^*$ of $(W_N)$: $W_{N_i}\to W^*$ with $N_1<N_2<\cdots$. If $W^*$ contained a letter at $k$ indices forming a progression, all inside the first $M$ letters, then for large $i$ (with $N_i\ge M$) $W_{N_i}$ agrees with $W^*$ on the first $M$ letters, so $W_{N_i}$'s first $N_i$ letters contain that progression, contradiction. Hence $W^*$ has no such progression, contradicting the original theorem. ∎

smt-2020-power-19.title: Long gaps give word-free tails
smt-2020-power-19.body:
*Finitely many occurrences:* let $M$ exceed all indices where $w$ appears; $W^*=T^M(W)$ (a T-limit with constant $n_i=M$) contains no $w$.

*Infinitely many occurrences with unbounded gaps:* the occurrence indices $i_1<i_2<\cdots$ have arbitrarily large gaps. For each $n$ pick consecutive occurrences $i_j<i_{j+1}$ with $i_{j+1}-i_j>n+|w|$, with $j=j(n)$ increasing in $n$, and let $U_n=T^{i_j+1}(W)$. Since $i_j,i_{j+1}$ are consecutive occurrences, no occurrence of $w$ begins at positions $0,\dots,n-1$ of $U_n$, so the prefix of $U_n$ of length $n$ contains no occurrence of $w$. By 16(c), $(U_n)$ has a strict limit $W^*$: $U_{n_i}\to W^*$ with $n_1<n_2<\cdots$; the truncation indices $i_{j(n_i)}+1$ increase, so $W^*$ is a T-limit of $W$. If $w$ appeared in $W^*$, within its first $M$ letters, then for $n_i\ge M$ the prefix of length $M$ of $U_{n_i}$ would contain $w$, contradicting the above. ∎

smt-2020-power-20a.title: Induction on $j$
smt-2020-power-20a.body:
*Lemma.* If $W'$ is a T-limit of $W$ and the word $f$ densely populates $W$ with all gaps $\le C$, then $f$ densely populates $W'$. Indeed every window of $W$ of length $C+|f|$ contains $f$, every finite subword of $W'$ appears in $W$ (15(b)), so every window of $W'$ of length $C+|f|$ contains $f$.

*Claim.* For $j\ge i$: $f_i$ is either absent from $W_j$ or dense in $W_j$. For $j=i$: if $f_i$ sparsely populates $W_{i-1}$ then $W_i$ is chosen without $f_i$ (absent); otherwise $f_i$ is dense in $W_{i-1}=W_i$. For $j>i$: $W_j$ is a T-limit of $W_{j-1}$ (or equal), so subwords of $W_j$ are subwords of $W_{j-1}$: if $f_i$ is absent from $W_{j-1}$ it is absent from $W_j$; if it is dense in $W_{j-1}$ it is dense in $W_j$ by the lemma. ∎

smt-2020-power-20b.title: Strict limit of the $W_i$
smt-2020-power-20b.body:
Each $W_i$ is a T-limit of $W_{i-1}$, hence $W_i\prec W_{i-1}\prec\cdots\prec W$ (inclusion $\prec$ is transitive). By 16(c) there is a strict limit $W_{\min}$ of $(W_i)$: $W_{n_t}\to W_{\min}$, $n_1<n_2<\cdots$. Every finite subword of $W_{\min}$ lies in the first $M$ letters, so it is a subword of $W_{n_t}$ for large $t$, hence of $W_i$ for every $i$ ($W_{n_t}\prec W_i$ when $n_t\ge i$) and of $W$: $W_{\min}\prec W_i$ for all $i$, and $W_{\min}\prec W$.

Let a finite word $f=f_i$ appear in $W_{\min}$. Then it appears in $W_i$, so by 20(a) it densely populates $W_i$, with gaps bounded by some $C$: every window of length $C+|f|$ of $W_i$ contains $f$. Every finite subword of $W_{\min}$ is a subword of $W_i$, so every window of $W_{\min}$ of length $C+|f|$ contains $f$: $f$ densely populates $W_{\min}$. ∎

smt-2020-power-21.title: Windows
smt-2020-power-21.body:
Let $W'$ be a T-limit of $W$, so $W'\prec W$ (15(b)): every subword of $W'$ is a subword of $W$. Conversely let $v$ be a subword of $W$; it densely populates $W$ with bound $C$, so every subword of $W$ of length $C+|v|$ contains $v$. The prefix of $W'$ of length $C+|v|$ is a subword of $W$, hence contains $v$; so $v$ is a subword of $W'$. Thus the sets of subwords coincide.

If $v$ appears in $W'$, it appears in $W$, and the same argument shows every window of $W'$ of length $C+|v|$ is a subword of $W$ and contains $v$; so $v$ densely populates $W'$. ∎

smt-2020-power-22a.title: Use a long repeated word
smt-2020-power-22a.body: $w$ appears with gaps $\le C$, so every subword of $W$ of length $m=C+|w|$ contains $w$. By hypothesis some word $v$ of length $m$ appears at indices $a,a+d,\dots,a+(k-1)d$. Since $v$ contains $w$, say at offset $s$, $w$ appears at the indices $a+s,a+s+d,\dots,a+s+(k-1)d$, an arithmetic progression. ∎

smt-2020-power-22b.title: Nested words
smt-2020-power-22b.body: Let $u_1$ be a letter of $W$. Given a word $u_i$ appearing in $W$, it appears at indices $s,s+d,\dots,s+(k-1)d$; let $u_{i+1}=W[s,\,s+(k-1)d+|u_i|)$, the stretch of $W$ covering all $k$ copies. Then $u_{i+1}$ appears in $W$, begins with $u_i$, and contains $u_i$ at the offsets $0,d,\dots,(k-1)d$. So the words $u_i$ are nested prefixes of each other; let $W^*$ be the infinite word having all $u_i$ as prefixes. Every finite subword of $W^*$ lies in some $u_i$, which appears in $W$: $W^*\prec W$. Every prefix $w$ of $W^*$ is a prefix of some $u_i$, which appears at offsets $0,d,\dots,(k-1)d$ in $u_{i+1}$, a prefix of $W^*$; so $w$ appears in $W^*$ at those offsets, an arithmetic progression starting at index $0$. ∎

smt-2020-power-23a.title: Choose $d$ from the prefix property
smt-2020-power-23a.body: Let $m'=\max\{x,y:(x,y)\in S\}+m$ and $d=n(m')$. The length-$m'$ prefix $P$ of $W^*$ appears at $0,d,\dots,(k-1)d$. For $(x,y)\in S$ and $k_1\in\{0,\dots,k-1\}$, the letters of $W^*$ at positions $x+k_1d,\dots,x+k_1d+m-1$ are the letters of the $k_1$-th copy of $P$ at offsets $x,\dots,x+m-1<m'$, i.e. the letters $W^*_x,\dots,W^*_{x+m-1}$. Likewise for $y+k_2d$. Since $x\sim y$ these coincide, so $x+k_1d\sim y+k_2d$. ∎

smt-2020-power-23b.title: Definitions
smt-2020-power-23b.body: Taking $k_1=k_2=0$ in $\{(a,a)\}\oplus d'\subseteq S$ shows $(a,a)\in S$. Hence $\{(a,a)\}\oplus d\subseteq S\oplus d$ (the elements $(a+k_1d,a+k_2d)$ come from $(a,a)\in S$). For the second: an element of $\{(a,a)\}\oplus(d+d')$ is $(a+k_1(d+d'),a+k_2(d+d'))=\bigl((a+k_1d')+k_1d,\ (a+k_2d')+k_2d\bigr)$, and $(a+k_1d',a+k_2d')\in S$ because $\{(a,a)\}\oplus d'\subseteq S$; with $k_1,k_2\in\{0,\dots,k-1\}$ this lies in $S\oplus d$. ∎

smt-2020-power-23c.title: Induction
smt-2020-power-23c.body: Note $S_{i+1}=S_i^+\oplus d_{i+1}\subseteq\Omega$ by the choice of $d_{i+1}$. We show $\{(a_i,a_i)\}\oplus\delta_{ij}\subseteq S_j$ by induction on $j>i$. For $j=i+1$: $(a_i,a_i)\in S_i^+$, so $\{(a_i,a_i)\}\oplus d_{i+1}\subseteq S_i^+\oplus d_{i+1}=S_{i+1}$. For $j\to j+1$: by hypothesis $\{(a_i,a_i)\}\oplus\delta_{ij}\subseteq S_j\subseteq S_j^+$, so by 23(b) with $S=S_j^+$, $d'=\delta_{ij}$, $d=d_{j+1}=d(S_j^+)$: $\{(a_i,a_i)\}\oplus(d_{j+1}+\delta_{ij})\subseteq S_j^+\oplus d_{j+1}=S_{j+1}$, and $d_{j+1}+\delta_{ij}=\delta_{i,j+1}$. Finally $S_j\subseteq\Omega$. ∎

smt-2020-power-23d.title: Pigeonhole
smt-2020-power-23d.body: There are at most $r^m$ words of length $m$, so among $a_0,a_1,\dots,a_{r^m}$ two indices satisfy $a_i\sim a_j$ with $i<j$. Put $\delta=\delta_{ij}\ge1$. By 23(c), for $t,t'\in\{0,\dots,k-1\}$, $a_i+t\delta\sim a_i+t'\delta$, so the $k$ indices $a_i,a_i+\delta,\dots,a_i+(k-1)\delta$ all carry the same length-$m$ word, and $a_i+k\delta=a_j\sim a_i$ carries it too. These $k+1$ indices form an arithmetic progression. ∎

smt-2020-power-24.title: Colour by the next element
smt-2020-power-24.body: Let all gaps be less than $C$. For $x\in\mathbb N$ let $c(x)=\min\{s\in S:s\ge x\}-x\in\{0,1,\dots,C-1\}$. This is a colouring with $C$ colours, so by van der Waerden's theorem some colour $c_0$ contains arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions $x,x+d,\dots,x+(L-1)d$. For every term, $x+jd+c_0\in S$ (the next element of $S$ at or after $x+jd$ is $x+jd+c_0$). So $x+c_0,\ x+c_0+d,\dots,x+c_0+(L-1)d$ is an arithmetic progression of length $L$ inside $S$. ∎

smt-2020-power-25.title: Finitary vdW
smt-2020-power-25.body: Let $|a_i-b_i|\le C$ and let $L$ be given. Put $N=N(2C+1,L)$ and take an arithmetic progression of length $N$ in $\{a_i\}$: $a_{i_t}=u+td$, $t=0,\dots,N-1$ (indices $i_t$ increasing). Colour $t$ by $b_{i_t}-a_{i_t}\in\{-C,\dots,C\}$ ($2C+1$ colours). By the finitary theorem there are $t_0$ and $s\ge1$ with $b_{i_{t_0+js}}-a_{i_{t_0+js}}=e$ constant for $j=0,\dots,L-1$. Then $b_{i_{t_0+js}}=u+(t_0+js)d+e=(u+t_0d+e)+j(sd)$ for $j<L$, an arithmetic progression of length $L$ in $\{b_i\}$. ∎

smt-2020-power-26a.title: Use a 3-term progression
smt-2020-power-26a.body:
Let $y=x/2$ and choose $M>2/\varepsilon$. Colour $n\in\mathbb N$ by $j$ if $\{n^2y\}\in[\frac jM,\frac{j+1}M)$. By van der Waerden there are $n$ and $k\ge1$ with $n,n+k,n+2k$ the same colour. Write $n^2y=A+f_1$, $(n+k)^2y=B+f_2$, $(n+2k)^2y=C+f_3$ with integers $A,B,C$ and $f_i$ in one interval of length $\frac1M$. Then
$$2k^2y=(n+2k)^2y-2(n+k)^2y+n^2y=(C-2B+A)+(f_3-2f_2+f_1),$$
and $|f_3-2f_2+f_1|<\frac2M<\varepsilon$ (write $f_i=c+g_i$ with $0\le g_i<\frac1M$; then $f_3-2f_2+f_1=g_3-2g_2+g_1\in(-\frac2M,\frac2M)$). Since $2k^2y=k^2x$, we get $\langle k^2x\rangle<\varepsilon$. ∎

smt-2020-power-26b.title: Reduce to fractional parts
smt-2020-power-26b.body:
Let $\alpha=1/x\in(0,1)$, irrational. We have $\lfloor nx\rfloor=s^2$ iff $s^2\le nx<s^2+1$ iff $s^2\alpha\le n<s^2\alpha+\alpha$. Since $s^2\alpha\notin\mathbb Z$, such an integer $n$ exists (namely $n=\lceil s^2\alpha\rceil$) iff $\{s^2\alpha\}>1-\alpha$. So it suffices to find infinitely many positive integers $s$ with $\{s^2\alpha\}>1-\alpha$; they give infinitely many distinct squares $s^2=\lfloor nx\rfloor$.

*Finding such $s$.* Let $0<\varepsilon<\alpha/4$ and by 26(a) take $k$ with $\langle k^2\alpha\rangle<\varepsilon$ (and $\langle k^2\alpha\rangle>0$ by irrationality). If $\{k^2\alpha\}>1-\varepsilon>1-\alpha$, take $s=k$. Otherwise $k^2\alpha=N+\eta$ with an integer $N$ and $0<\eta<\varepsilon$. For $a\ge1$, $(ak)^2\alpha=a^2N+a^2\eta$, so $\{(ak)^2\alpha\}=\{a^2\eta\}$. Let $a$ be the largest integer with $a^2\eta<1$; then $a<\eta^{-1/2}$ and $(a+1)^2\eta\ge1$, so $a^2\eta\ge1-(2a+1)\eta>1-2\sqrt\eta-\eta>1-2\sqrt\varepsilon-\varepsilon$. If $\varepsilon$ is small enough that $2\sqrt\varepsilon+\varepsilon<\alpha$, then $\{(ak)^2\alpha\}>1-\alpha$ and we take $s=ak$.

*Infinitely many $s$.* Letting $\varepsilon\to0$, the corresponding $k$ must tend to infinity (for fixed $k$, $\langle k^2\alpha\rangle>0$ since $\alpha$ is irrational), and $s\ge k$. Hence there are infinitely many $s$, hence infinitely many squares of the form $\lfloor n\pi^{2020}\rfloor$. ∎
